content: The eyelid is a delicate and thin fold of skin that serves to cover and protect the eye. It is one of the thinnest areas of skin on the human body, second only to the prepuce and labia minora. The levator palpebrae superioris muscle is responsible for retracting the eyelid to open the eye, a process that can occur both voluntarily and involuntarily. Human eyelids are equipped with a row of eyelashes, which enhance the protection of the eye by preventing dust and foreign particles from entering. The term palpebral (or blepharo) refers specifically to the eyelids. Anatomy of the Eyelid Layers The human eyelid is composed of several distinct layers, arranged from superficial to deep: the skin, subcutaneous tissue, orbicularis oculi muscle, orbital septum and tarsal plates, and the palpebral conjunctiva. Embedded within the eyelid are the meibomian glands, which secrete the lipid component of the tear film, essential for maintaining eye moisture and preventing tear evaporation. Skin The skin of the eyelid is similar to other areas of the body but contains a higher concentration of pigment cells. In certain pathological conditions, these pigment cells may migrate, leading to discoloration of the eyelids. The skin also contains sweat glands and hair follicles, with the latter forming eyelashes at the eyelid margin. Innervation The sensory innervation of the upper eyelid is provided by the infratrochlear, supratrochlear, supraorbital, and lacrimal nerves, all of which are branches of the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V). The lower eyelid receives sensory input from the infratrochlear nerve at the medial angle and branches of the infraorbital nerve, which is part of the maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve. Blood Supply The eyelids are vascularized by two arterial arches in both the upper and lower lids. These arches are formed by anastomoses between the lateral palpebral arteries (branches of the lacrimal artery) and the medial palpebral arteries (branches of the ophthalmic artery). Muscles In addition to the orbicularis oculi muscle, which facilitates eyelid closure, there are involuntary muscle fibers controlled by the sympathetic autonomic nervous system that help widen the eye aperture. The corrugator supercilii muscle protects the eye from sunlight by drawing the eyebrows toward the nose, creating a roof over the medial side of the eye and forming characteristic forehead furrows. The procerus muscle, located on the nasal bridge, creates transverse furrows in the skin. The frontalis muscle elevates the eyebrows, counteracting the orbital portion of the orbicularis oculi, particularly during upward gaze or when viewing distant or dim objects. Functions of the Eyelid Blinking, the rapid closure and reopening of the eyelid, serves to spread moisture across the eye's surface, alleviating dryness and discomfort. It also helps remove irritants that may have entered the eye. A deliberate blink of one eye, known as winking, is often used as a social signal. Most animals with eyelids exhibit a reflexive closure of the eyes when a threat approaches, protecting the eye from potential contact. This reflex is typically strong enough to override voluntary resistance. Eyelids also regulate the amount of light entering the eye, complementing the autonomic control of the iris. Without eyelids, many animals would be unable to shield their eyes from excessive light or visual sensory overload. Additionally, eyelids block light during sleep cycles, aiding in rest. Types of Eyelids Humans possess both upper and lower eyelids, which function as a pair. However, it is primarily the upper eyelid that moves across the eye's surface during blinking. In most animals, the lower eyelid moves vertically. Many terrestrial vertebrates have a third eyelid, known as the nictitating membrane or haw, which is located closer to the eye than the outer lids and is often transparent. This membrane provides additional protection against debris and irritation and serves as a barrier during swimming in land animals. Examples of animals with a nictitating membrane include camels, crocodiles, cats, birds, and polar bears. The membrane moves diagonally or horizontally across the eye. In humans, the plica semilunaris (or semilunar fold) is thought to be a vestigial remnant of this structure. Eyelids are believed to have evolved as a mechanism to remove debris from the eyes. Since fish have a constant flow of water over their eyes, they lack eyelids or specialized membranes for this purpose. Double Eyelid A double eyelid is characterized by the presence of a crease, whereas a single eyelid lacks such a crease. The location of the crease varies widely, particularly in individuals with an Asian double eyelid. Cultural Practices Related to Eyelids After death, it is a common cultural practice in many societies to close the eyes of the deceased by pulling the eyelids down. This is a traditional part of the last offices performed for the deceased.
